title: Filovirus -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Filoviruses represent a group of viruses that are capable of causing severe and often fatal illnesses in humans. Characterized by symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhea, and, less frequently, hemorrhaging and coma, these infections carry high morbidity and mortality. Ebola virus disease, the most well-known filovirus infection, poses significant challenges for both clinical care and public health systems, especially during outbreaks. Rapid identification, isolation, and supportive care remain crucial to reducing transmission and improving survival. The unpredictable nature of outbreaks and potential for widespread impact highlight the urgency of preparedness, coordinated response, and community engagement to limit disease spread.

title: Filovirus -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Through this course, participants gain a thorough understanding of the diagnosis, clinical features, and evidence-based management of filovirus infections, with an emphasis on Ebola virus disease. The content highlights the importance of collaboration among infectious disease specialists, frontline clinicians, nurses, laboratory teams, epidemiologists, and public health authorities. By coordinating surveillance, implementing infection control protocols, and sharing timely data, the interprofessional team improves early detection, reduces transmission, and supports patient-centered care. This integrated approach ultimately strengthens outbreak response and improves patient outcomes.

title: Filovirus -- Introduction
content: Filoviruses, a viral family, Filoviridae , can cause hemorrhagic fever in humans and primates.  There are 3 known genera of filoviruses: Cuevavirus, Marburgvirus, and Ebolavirus. These further subdivide into 6 species: Zaire, Sudan, Tai Forest, Bundibugyo, Reston, and Bombali.  Thus far, the Reston and Bombali strains are not known to cause disease in humans. [1]

title: Filovirus -- Introduction
content: Structurally, filoviruses obtained their name due to their macroscopic appearance as filamentous viruses, from the Latin "filum" for "thread," often having a string-like or torus-like appearance.  They have enveloped particles that contain a negative-sense, single-stranded RNA genome with genes arranged linearly. Additionally, they have a single glycoprotein spike on the surface and 4 structural proteins, which include the virus-encoded polymerase. [1] Filoviruses are highly contagious and spread quickly via human-to-human contact. They are considered biosafety level 4 agents with very high mortality rates. [2]

title: Filovirus -- Etiology
content: The Ebola virus infects a broad range of cell types.  After attachment to the host cell, mediated by the surface glycoprotein, the virus gets internalized via macropinocytosis.  The binding efficacy of the virus is related to acid sphingomyelinase and plasma membrane sphingomyelin on the host cell. [3] On the viral side, attachment gets mediated via its glycoprotein, a triplet of heterodimers each containing a binding and fusion subunit.  Once internalized into the host cell, the virus travels into the late endosome, where the cysteine protease activates the fusogenic form of the surface glycoprotein, which exposes the binding domain and results in fusion of the viral envelope with the endosome membrane, releasing the viral nucleocapsid into the cytoplasm with resultant transcription, replication, and budding of new viruses.  After infection begins, the virus spreads to multiple cell types, resulting in generalized organ failure. [2] See Figure. Filovirus.

title: Filovirus -- Epidemiology
content: The first discovery of filovirus was in 1976. Since then, it has been associated with over twenty known outbreaks, primarily located in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly in isolated rural areas, with a focus on Sudan, Uganda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Gabon. To date, the largest known outbreak occurred in West Africa from 2013 to 2016. This outbreak involved multiple countries, both rural and urban areas, and had a high mortality rate, with over 28000 infections and 11,000 deaths. However, this number may be optimistic as the actual number is thought to be much higher due to under-reporting.  Thus far, the Ebola virus outbreaks in humans have been confined to African countries, but this could change easily with international travel, and secondary cases have been reported in Spain and the USA.

title: Filovirus -- Epidemiology
content: Ebolavirus is zoonotic, with fruit bats of the Pteropodidae family currently considered the natural hosts of the disease. In natural conditions, scientists have yet to isolate the virus in bats.  Transmission to humans is likely to occur through the handling of sick/infected forest animals.  Secondary spread via human-human transmission occurs via direct contact with infected body fluids.

title: Filovirus -- Pathophysiology
content: The virus enters the body through mucous membranes and infects cells such as macrophages and dendritic cells. The filovirus then replicates within the host, causing necrosis and the subsequent release of thousands of new viral particles into the body. The virus then spreads systemically in a rapid fashion by suppressing the Type I interferon response. Systemic spread to lymph nodes, spleen, liver, thymus, and other immunologic tissues results in further virus propagation. Autopsies show that fatal disease usually results in necrosis of the tissues of organs such as the liver and spleen. [1] The body reacts to filovirus infection through a systemic inflammatory response, releasing various cytokines that can contribute to symptoms such as shock, nausea, vomiting, vascular leak, coagulation defects, and volume depletion. [3]

title: Filovirus -- History and Physical
content: A thorough patient history and physical examination are essential for the diagnosis and evaluation of any disease. For filoviruses, special care must be taken regarding travel history, exposure history, and sick contacts. Obtaining the type, duration, and onset of symptoms is necessary. Generalized symptoms include prodromal fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle pain, weakness, fatigue, headache, abdominal pain, and unexplained hemorrhage.  Symptoms generally appear 2 to 21 days after contact (with an average of 8 to 10 days) and are commonly mistaken for the flu or malaria. Hemorrhagic symptoms can vary and occur in approximately 30 to 50% of patients and often include mucosal bleeding, particularly involving the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts. [4]

title: Filovirus -- Evaluation
content: In addition to the history and physical exam, general lab tests typically demonstrate signs of intravascular volume depletion from gastrointestinal volume losses, along with extensive liver and renal laboratory abnormalities. Indirect identification of viral particles, proteins, or RNA from blood, serum, or plasma is used for the diagnosis of filovirus infection, with RNA nucleic acid amplification testing being the preferred method.  These tests pose a significant risk of lab-acquired infections, and patient samples are an extreme biohazard risk, requiring special laboratory procedures. Definitive confirmation of infection is only by virus isolation. IgM testing can be diagnostic during the convalescent phase of illness, and IgG is generally only monitored for epidemiologic surveillance. Rapid diagnostic tests were developed in response to the 2014 Ebola outbreak, with 5 tests approved for the Ebola virus.  These tests utilize the same antibody/antigen capture method as an ELISA test, but are performed in a lateral flow strip, allowing for faster results with less processing.  Rapid testing is critical in controlling outbreaks and preventing the spread of the virus. [1]

title: Filovirus -- Treatment / Management
content: Managing filovirus disease typically focuses on prevention and detection, with other management strategies beginning to emerge.  There are very few randomized controlled trials on the treatment of Ebola.  With only 1 specific anti-Ebola therapy, ZMapp, which enrolled 72 patients and compared ZMapp, a monoclonal antibody, with standard care, resulting in 22% vs 37% mortality.  Another international, multisite retrospective cohort study has examined intravenous fluid therapy compared to oral hydration and found no statistically significant difference in 28-day survival among the 424 participants studied. [5]

title: Filovirus -- Treatment / Management
content: Studies have examined convalescent plasma with unclear results.  Two studies revealed decreased mortality rates with convalescent plasma (31% vs 38% and 28% vs 44%), but these studies had limitations, including a lack of randomization, insufficient data on other interventions, and an unknown level of neutralizing antibodies in the plasma. Their small sample sizes also limited the scope of these studies.

title: Filovirus -- Treatment / Management
content: A non-randomized single-arm study involving 99 patients was conducted to evaluate favipiravir. Patients tolerated it well, with a 44% reduction in mortality compared to 65%; however, this data is limited by small sample sizes, non-randomization, and a lack of control for between-group treatments. [6] Interferon beta 1-a has been studied in a non-randomized single-arm study and found a reduction in 21-day mortality from 84% to 33%. Data limitations included a small sample size and non-randomization. [6] Also, palliative care has been suggested as an essential element for the treatment of these diseases, given their high fatality rate, lack of effective treatment, and the crisis nature of outbreaks.  Palliative services are critical to preventing and alleviating the suffering of patients in such a high-fatality disease with significant additional psycho-social strain associated with outbreaks, infection, and symptom burden. [5]

title: Filovirus -- Treatment / Management
content: Other molecular studies have identified agents not specific to the Ebola virus that may aid in treatment.  Ion channel inhibitors, such as amiodarone, have shown an affinity for preventing filovirus entry into cells in vitro ; this inhibition is attainable at normal treatment doses for arrhythmia.  Additionally, amiodarone interferes with glycoprotein processing, resulting in the inhibition of viral envelope fusion with the endosomal membrane.  However, these in vitro studies have not shown any clinical improvements in treatment during outbreaks.  Antiparasitic drugs, such as chloroquine, have been shown to have antiviral properties by inhibiting viral entry and reducing inflammation.  However, despite promising in vitro studies, human studies have not demonstrated the efficacy of antiparasitic drugs in the Ebola virus infection.  Psychoactive drugs, such as chlorpromazine and first-generation antihistamines, also act by inhibiting viral internalization.  Selective estrogen receptor modulators also inhibit viral entry, independent of estrogen receptors on target cells, with the exact mechanism remaining unknown. Two animal studies have shown promise for protection from Ebola virus infection, with 1 confirming protection and the other achieving 50% protection rates. [7] [8]

title: Filovirus -- Treatment / Management
content: During the 2014-2016 outbreak, 2 vaccines underwent phase II/III trials and showed promise with high efficacy and long-term antibody responses for the Ebola virus.  Marburgvirus, another filovirus, does not have a vaccine to date. [9]

title: Filovirus -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Ebola virus and Marburg virus disease must be considered in patients who have traveled to areas where they are endemic or have had reported outbreaks. Nonspecific viral prodrome and fever make a specific diagnosis difficult, and filovirus infection can be easily mistaken for malaria, typhoid fever, influenza, Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, an acute surgical abdomen, cholera, and other hemorrhagic fevers such as dengue, Lassa, and yellow fever. [9]

title: Filovirus -- Toxicity and Adverse Effect Management
content: Treatment of filoviral infection primarily involves supportive care, including fluid and electrolyte replacement, respiratory support, and antimicrobial therapy. A few investigative therapies are currently under development. [10]

title: Filovirus -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis for filovirus infection tends to be quite poor, with few treatment options and high mortality rates that vary between 30% and 70% with prognosis worsening with increasing patient age and nutritional status. Notably, vaccines have undergone Phase II/III clinical trials during the 2014-2016 outbreak. [9]

title: Filovirus -- Complications
content: In severe forms of the disease, death usually occurs around 6 to 16 days from symptom onset.  The cause of death is typically shock and multiorgan failure, primarily hepatic and renal failure, also including thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy. [6]

title: Filovirus -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Public health interventions should aim to contain the epidemic and minimize transmission in both healthcare settings and the community.  Additionally, to the coordinated local response, the World Health Organization, under the Global Outbreak Alert and Response network, coordinates a global response.  Outbreak containment has seen success in Uganda due to strong political support with the development of local task forces, public education, effective coordination, prompt utilization of community resources, and efficient laboratory systems. Cases of confirmed or suspected filovirus infection should undergo management in isolated facilities within affected communities. [11]

title: Filovirus -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patients should receive education regarding the risks and high mortality associated with filovirus infection, along with routes of spread, including bodily fluids and sexual transmission.  Additionally, the importance of reporting suspected cases should be reinforced, and home treatment should also be strongly discouraged. [12]

title: Filovirus -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Management of filovirus disease and an outbreak is an interprofessional undertaking that requires the mobilization of not only resources within the hospital managing the patient, but also local resources to contain the spread of the disease, identify infected individuals, and educate the population. National and global resources, such as the Centers for Disease Control and the World Health Organization, assist in managing local cases, identifying the outbreak's origin, preventing its spread, providing diagnostic aid from high-level biosafety laboratories, and offering experimental treatment options. [13]

title: Filovirus -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Within the hospital, multiple specialists are needed to coordinate the care of critically ill patients requiring input from gastroenterology, nephrology, infectious disease, hematology, specialty-trained nursing, pharmacy, among many others.  Infectious disease board-certified pharmacists can assist with supportive measures or cutting-edge, unproven therapies if desired. Nursing provides supportive care and monitors the patient's condition, reporting any changes in status to the team. Furthermore, coordination of containment within the hospital and minimization of lab draws and, therefore, of exposure risks for healthcare workers is essential given the possibility of laboratory-acquired infection and person-to-person transmission. Thus, an interprofessional team approach is needed for both care and containment. [6]
